Part 01

Introduction

Part 01 — Introduction

Agility ≠ Change of Direction Speed

CODS
Pre-programmed rapid whole-body movement with change of velocity/direction. Known pattern. Closed skill.
Agility
The same movement, in response to a stimulus. Unplanned. Open skill. A real perceptual-cognitive demand.
Part 01 — Introduction

What Is Missing?

Perception & Decision-Making
Traditional COD tests carry no perceptual-cognitive demand — there's nothing to read, only a known pattern to execute.
Skill-Level Discrimination
Closed drills tend to tell the same story across ability levels. Reaction is what separates a starter from a backup.
Transfer to Competition
A testing and training construct only matters if it transfers to what actually happens in a game.
Part 01 — Introduction

Research Insight

Study Design
12 first-team and 30 second-team rugby league players were run through a battery of reactive-agility drills alongside traditional, pre-planned change-of-direction tests.
Finding
Only the reactive tests picked up a meaningful gap between the two squads — the pre-planned tests couldn't tell first-team players from second-team players.
Why it matters: a test that can't separate a starter from a backup isn't measuring what actually matters on the field.

Gabbett, T. J., Kelly, J. N., & Sheppard, J. M. (2008). Speed, change of direction speed, and reactive agility of rugby league players. Journal of Strength and Conditioning Research, 22(1), 174–181. DOI: 10.1519/JSC.0b013e31815ef700

Photo by Olga Guryanova on Unsplash

Part 02 — Technical Model

Movement Skills vs. Sport Skills

Movement Skills
Single pattern or pattern sequence, learned in isolation — non-reactive or reactive, no sport context attached yet.
Sport Skills
The same single pattern or pattern sequence, now performed against a generic or sport-specific stimulus.
Why It Matters
A drill only becomes a sport skill once it's tested against a stimulus that matches the sport — not just any reaction cue.

Part 02 — Technical Model · Change of Direction

Deceleration: The Foundational Skill

Mechanics
Lower center of gravity, feet ahead of COG, forefoot initial contact, full ankle→knee→hip shock-absorption chain.
The Fault
Flat-footed, straight-knee landings — a flagged ACL-risk pattern.
Correct — Low COM, Wide Base
Incorrect — Extreme Flexion
Part 02 — Technical Model · Change of Direction

Critical Position 1 — Base Position

Spine & Base
Neutral spine position. Base width and depth set relative to sport demands.
Loading & Balance
Weight loaded on the inside edge of the shoes. Center of mass balanced within the base.
Part 02 — Technical Model · Change of Direction

Critical Position 2 — Shuffle/Cut

Shuffle / Cut
Low base > shoulder width. Outside-leg push through inside-edge loading. Inside leg hovers under inside shoulder.
The Sequence
Eccentric → isometric → concentric, every rep.
Part 02 — Technical Model · Change of Direction

Critical Position 3 — Crossover

Crossover
Inside-leg push through outside-edge loading. Outside leg snaps tight across body. Shoulder/arm rotation counters hip rotation.
The Sequence
Eccentric → isometric → concentric, every rep.

Coaching & Drills
Part 02 — Technical Model · Reactive Agility

Reactive Agility, Defined

The Definition
Rapid whole-body movement, change of velocity/direction, in response to a stimulus.
Reaction Speed
Latency period. Simple vs. selective stimulus. Acoustic / visual / tactile receptor channels.
Physical qualities transfer well to CODS — the evidence for them transferring to true reactive agility is much weaker. The reactive/decision-making element has to be trained directly, not assumed as a byproduct.
Part 02 — Technical Model · Reactive Agility

The Decision Cycle

Observe
Observe the cue
Orient

Decide & Act
Decide, then act
Part 03

Coaching
Model

The Coaching Pyramid, the verbal cues, and the applied drills for both Change of Direction and Reactive Agility.

Part 03 — Coaching Model

The Coaching Pyramid

Tier 1 · Posture
Center of mass vs. base — the foundation everything else is built on.
Tier 2 · Leg Action
Inside leg vs. outside leg — which one pushes, which one snaps.
Tier 3 · Arm Action
Rotation and balance — the last correction layer, not the first.
Part 03 — Coaching Model

Shuffle/Cut Cues

Outside Leg
"Push, drive, snap — punch the ground away." "Explode off the ground." "Weight inside the cut."
Posture
"Angle in, angle out." "Stay under the roof." "Wide base."
Part 03 — Coaching Model

Crossover Cues

Inside Leg
"Push, drive, snap — punch the ground away." "Explode off the ground."
Outside Leg
"Snap the knee across, like breaking a pane of glass." "Drive the knee toward the target direction."
Part 03 — Coaching Model

Coaching the Reactive Layer

Layer auditory or visual stimuli onto existing COD drills — don't build a wholly separate drill category from scratch.

Cueing example: "Keep them in your headlights" — a hip-reading cue for defensive/reactive positioning. Targets the "orient" stage of the decision cycle specifically.

Programming and
Periodisation

Programming and Periodisation

100m Sprint Progression

A 30-week short-to-long sprint progression for the 100m — drills and short-distance work taper as phases shift toward race-distance emphasis.

Programming and Periodisation

Team Sport Progression

A 12-to-16 week short-to-long sprint progression for team sports — compressed compared to the 100m model, since team-sport efforts rarely exceed 40m.

10 m emphasis
